title: Learning What Matters Now: Dynamic Preference Inference under Contextual Shifts
claim: An agent's priorities between competing values shift as contextual pressure changes, so a fixed objective weighting fails to capture behavior.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right in time, dashed dividers, value-weight bars below
description: Three side-by-side panels, separated by dashed vertical lines, show time steps t1, t2 and t3 of a queueing scene. In each panel, cartoon people stand in line toward a food stall with a chef. A labeled blue 'Agent' tag marks the first person, and a thought bubble holds the agent's inner monologue. The bubbles read 'It's still early, no need to rush,' then 'Hold on, it's almost my turn,' then 'Time is running out. I need to get ahead in line.' Under each scene is a horizontal stacked bar for value weights, with yellow for Energy and blue for Morality. The splits are 0.3/0.7, 0.5/0.5 and 0.8/0.2. A legend sits at the left. The eye goes first to the cartoon line, then down to the bars.
caption: Adaptive value preference adjustment in a queueing scenario. At early stages (t1), the agent prioritizes morality and chooses to wait. As the deadline approaches (t2), preferences between morality (M) and energy (E) become balanced. When time is nearly exhausted (t3), energy becomes dominant and the agent rationalizes cutting in line, illustrating dynamic reweighting of values under changing pressures.
abstract: Humans often juggle multiple, sometimes conflicting objectives and shift their priorities as circumstances change, rather than following a fixed objective function. In contrast, most computational decision-making and multi-objective RL methods assume static preference weights or a known scalar reward. In this work, we study sequential decision-making problem when these preference weights are unobserved latent variables that drift with context. Specifically, we propose Dynamic Preference Inference (DPI), a cognitively inspired framework in which an agent maintains a probabilistic belief over preference weights, updates this belief from recent interaction, and conditions its policy on inferred preferences. We instantiate DPI as a variational preference inference module trained jointly with a preference-conditioned actor-critic, using vector-valued returns as evidence about latent trade-offs. In queueing, maze, and multi-objective continuous-control environments with event-driven changes in objectives, DPI adapts its inferred preferences to new regimes and achieves higher post-shift performance than fixed-weight and heuristic envelope baselines.
